name: Rat Distortion
description:
The Pro Co RAT. Hard clipping, a filter knob that works backwards, and one of the three or four genuinely distinct distortion sounds that exist.

The LM308 op-amp at its heart is deliberately slow, which rounds off the harshest edges and gives the RAT its thick, slightly compressed grind. The Filter control removes treble as you turn it up — clockwise is darker, which catches everyone out once.

Jeff Beck, Thom Yorke, Kurt Cobain, Dave Grohl. It sits somewhere between an overdrive and a fuzz and sounds like neither.

name: PI Fuzz
description:
The Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi, in its current production form.

Four transistor stages, enormous sustain and a tone control that scoops the midrange out in the middle of its travel — which is why a Muff can sound huge alone and vanish completely in a band. Keep the tone knob off centre.

Gilmour's lead sound, Smashing Pumpkins' wall, and every stoner rock record ever made.

name: Tube Drive 3-Knob
description:
The Butler Tube Driver, which has a real 12AX7 valve running at high voltage inside a stompbox.

That makes it behave like an amp stage rather than a clipping circuit: it compresses under your hands, it gets warmer as you push it, and it never gets harsh. This is the three-knob version.

Eric Johnson's violin lead sound is a Tube Driver into a Marshall, and David Gilmour has used one since the eighties.

name: Super OD
description:
The BOSS SD-1, which is a Tube Screamer with one diode changed.

That change makes the clipping asymmetrical, which sounds subtly rougher and more open than the symmetrical version. It has been the cheapest good overdrive on Earth for forty years.

Zakk Wylde has used one in front of a JCM800 for his entire career.

name: Treble Boost
description:
A treble booster — a single transistor, a capacitor that throws away the low end, and a volume knob.

It was the standard trick for making a small British amp break up in the sixties, and it is the entire reason Brian May's AC30 sounds the way it does. Almost useless on its own and transformative in front of a valve amp.

name: Mid Boost
specs: Fractal original · no pedal behind it
description:
Fractal's own midrange boost, not a model of anything. A lift in the mids and nothing else.

Useful for the job a Tube Screamer is usually doing — pushing an amp's front end where it responds most — without the Screamer's character coming along with it.

name: T808 OD
description:
The Ibanez TS-808 Tube Screamer, and the most argued-about nine volts in music.

What it actually does is cut low end, push the midrange forward and add a soft, symmetrical clip — which on its own sounds nasal and thin. In front of a cranked amp it is transformative: the bass that would have turned to mud is gone before it arrives, and what is left is tight and vocal.

Set the drive low and the level high. It is a tightening device far more often than it is a distortion.

name: Fat Rat
basedOn: modded Pro Co RAT with LED clipping
description:
A RAT with LEDs in place of the clipping diodes, which is the most common modification done to one.

LEDs clip at a higher voltage, so the pedal gets louder, cleaner and considerably more open before it distorts. More amp-like and less compressed than a stock RAT.

name: T808 Mod
description:
A modified TS-808 — the mods people have been doing to these since the eighties, which almost always mean more low end and more output.

The stock pedal's mid hump is the thing everyone loves and the thing everyone tries to remove. This is the version that keeps more of the guitar underneath it.

name: Octave Distortion
description:
The Tycobrahe Octavia, which adds an octave above the note as well as distorting it.

The octave only tracks cleanly on the neck pickup above the twelfth fret, which is exactly where Hendrix played the solo it is famous for. Elsewhere it is a strange, ring-modulated mess, which is also useful.

name: Plus Distortion
description:
The MXR Distortion+, and the sound of early Ozzy-era Randy Rhoads.

Two knobs and germanium diode clipping, which is softer and warmer than the silicon in most pedals. Not very much gain by modern standards — it works as a midrange-forward boost into an already-working amp.

name: Hard Fuzz
specs: Fractal original · no pedal behind it
description:
A hard-clipping fuzz of Fractal's own design rather than a model of a particular box.

Square-wave clipping with very little rounding, which is aggressive and slightly broken-sounding by intent.

name: FET Boost
specs: Fractal original · no pedal behind it
description:
A clean FET boost of Fractal's own design rather than a model of a particular pedal.

FET gain stages clip softly and asymmetrically, which is why they are used as front ends. This adds level and a little of that softness and nothing else.

name: Tape Distortion
description:
Not a pedal at all: the saturation of magnetic tape driven past what it can hold.

Tape compresses as it distorts and rolls the extreme top off as it goes, which is why loud records cut to tape sound bigger rather than harsher. A very different texture from any diode.

name: Full OD
description:
The Fulltone Full-Drive 2, and for a long stretch the default boutique overdrive on every pedalboard.

It is a Tube Screamer relative with a boost stage built in and a switch for flat mids — that switch removes the Screamer hump and is why people bought it.

name: Blues OD
description:
The Marshall Bluesbreaker: barely any gain, an enormous amount of warmth, and a pedal Marshall discontinued before realising what they had.

It is the ancestor of a whole family of transparent overdrives, and originals now sell for many times what they cost new.

name: Shred Distortion
description:
The Marshall Shredmaster: a proper three-band EQ, a lot of gain, and a voicing somewhere between a JCM800 and a RAT.

Radiohead built most of The Bends and OK Computer on one, which is not what Marshall had in mind.

name: M-Zone Distortion
description:
The BOSS Metal Zone, the most famous and most mocked distortion pedal ever built.

It has a huge amount of gain and a proper parametric midrange control — and it is mocked because the factory setting scoops those mids out entirely, which sounds enormous alone and disappears in a band.

Put the mids back and it is a genuinely capable high-gain pedal. That one knob is the difference.

name: Bender Fuzz
description:
The Tone Bender, which came before the Fuzz Face and is rougher, more aggressive and less polite about it.

Three transistor stages rather than two, with a harder, more spitting texture. Jimmy Page used one on the first two Led Zeppelin records.

name: BB Pre
description:
The Xotic BB Preamp — a clean boost and a Marshall-ish overdrive in one, with active bass and treble that can add as well as cut.

That active EQ is the difference. It will put low end back into a thin amp rather than only taking it away.

name: Master Fuzz
description:
The Maestro Fuzz-Tone, the first fuzz pedal ever sold, and for two years nobody bought one.

Then Keith Richards put it on Satisfaction as a placeholder for a horn section that never got recorded, and Gibson sold out of them within months.

It is thin, splatty and genuinely primitive, and no modern fuzz sounds like it.

name: Face Fuzz
description:
The Dallas-Arbiter Fuzz Face. Two transistors, two knobs, a circuit simple enough to sketch from memory, and the sound of the late sixties.

Its defining behaviour is how it responds to your guitar's volume knob: full up it is a thick, splatty fuzz, and rolled back to seven it cleans up into a warm overdrive. That interaction is the pedal. It only works properly straight into the guitar, with nothing buffered in front of it.

Hendrix, almost entirely. Everything anybody knows about fuzz came out of one man using one of these.

name: Bit Crusher
description:
Not a pedal and not analogue: this throws away bits of resolution and sample rate on purpose.

The result is the harsh, gritty, slightly metallic sound of early samplers and broken digital gear. Nothing that happens in a valve or a diode sounds like this.

name: Eternal Love
description:
The Lovepedal Eternity, a hand-built overdrive built on the Tube Screamer idea with germanium clipping and a lot more openness.

Warmer and less mid-humped than the pedal it descends from.

name: Esoteric ACB
description:
The Xotic AC Booster — the warmer, more overdriven half of the pair, voiced somewhere near a cranked class-A amp.

More gain and more midrange than the RC, with active bass and treble to shape it.

name: Esoteric RCB
description:
The Xotic RC Booster: a clean boost that adds level and a little sparkle and almost nothing else.

Its active EQ makes it a genuinely useful tone shaper rather than only a volume control. Very common as an always-on.

name: Zen Master
description:
The Hermida Zendrive, built to get a Dumble-ish sound out of an amp that is not a Dumble.

Smooth, vocal and extremely responsive to picking, with a voice control that shifts it from dark and thick to open and singing. Best set low and used as an always-on.

name: Tube Drive 4-Knob
description:
The four-knob Tube Driver, which adds a tone control to the original three.

Same valve, same amp-like behaviour, with one more way to shape it.

name: FAS LED-Drive
description:
Fractal's own overdrive built around LED clipping rather than a copy of an existing pedal.

LEDs clip at a higher voltage than diodes, so this stays open and loud rather than compressing — more headroom than most drives, and more of the guitar left underneath.

name: SDD Preamp
description:
The preamp section of the Korg SDD-3000 delay, which nobody set out to use as an effect until The Edge did.

His entire U2 sound runs through this front end — it adds a compressed, slightly hi-fi sheen and a lift in the upper mids that makes a clean guitar sound enormous before any delay arrives.

name: FET Preamp
basedOn: possibly based on the BOSS FA-1 FET Amplifier
description:
A FET preamp of the kind used as a front end rather than an effect — most likely the BOSS FA-1, which Andy Summers and The Edge both used.

It adds level and a bright, glassy lift and very little distortion.

name: Suhr Riot Ge (R)
description:
The Suhr Riot with germanium diodes selected — the softest and warmest of its three clipping options.

The Riot is a high-gain pedal built to sound like an amp rather than a box, and this setting is the most forgiving of the three.

name: Micro Boost
description:
The MXR Micro Amp: one knob, up to twenty-odd dB of gain, and no tone shaping at all.

It is the most honest boost in this list. Everything goes up and nothing changes, which is exactly what you want in front of an amp that is already right.

name: FAS Boost
specs: Fractal original · no pedal behind it
description:
Fractal's own clean boost. There is no pedal behind it and no story to tell about it.

It adds level with as little colour as the block can manage, which is exactly what you want in front of an amp that is already doing the right thing.

name: Timothy Mid
description:
The Paul Cochrane Timmy, which became a cult pedal entirely by word of mouth.

Its trick is that the bass and treble controls CUT rather than boost, so you subtract what the amp does not need and leave everything else alone. This is the middle setting, with both roughly flat.

One of the most transparent overdrives ever made, and it was never expensive.

name: Shimmer Drive
specs: Fractal original · no pedal behind it
description:
Fractal's own drive, voiced bright and harmonically busy rather than after any particular pedal.

It adds upper-harmonic content as it saturates, which is where the name comes from.

name: Blackglass 7K
description:
The Darkglass Microtubes B7K — a bass preamp and distortion with a blend and a proper four-band EQ, and the standard modern metal bass sound.

The blend is essential: distort the top and keep the clean low end underneath, or the bass disappears.

name: Suhr Riot LED (L)
description:
The Riot with LED clipping: more headroom, more volume and a more open, less compressed response.

The most amp-like of the three settings, and the loudest.

name: Timothy Up
description:
The Timmy with its cut controls opened up — more low end and more top than the middle setting, which makes it fuller and more amp-like.

The setting for a thin single-coil guitar.

name: Tone of Kings
description:
The Analog Man King of Tone: two independent overdrives in one box, and a waiting list that has run to years.

Each side can be set as boost, overdrive or distortion, and stacking them is the point. Warm, open and unfussy — closer to turning an amp up than to adding a pedal.

The waiting list is real and it is the reason this model exists.

name: Heartpedal 11
description:
Lovepedal's OD11 — considerably more gain than the Eternity and voiced towards a cranked British amp.

Closer to a distortion than an overdrive, with a thick midrange.

name: Jam Ray
description:
The Vemuram Jan Ray, built around the idea of a blackface Fender at the edge of breakup.

Very little gain and a great deal of low-end body, with a trim control for the amount of that Fender-ish push. Expensive, and much loved by players who mostly play clean.

name: Suhr Riot LED/Si (M)
description:
The Riot's middle setting, mixing LED and silicon clipping — more bite than germanium, more control than LEDs alone.

The setting most people end up leaving it on, and the one that suits a downtuned guitar best.

name: OD 250
description:
The DOD Overdrive Preamp 250, reissued. Two knobs, a lot of level on tap, and a bright, hard-edged boost.

Circuit-wise it is a close relative of the MXR Distortion+, with a different diode choice that makes it sharper.

name: Timothy Down
description:
The Timmy with the bass and treble cut hard, leaving a focused midrange.

This is the setting that turns it into a tightening boost in front of a high-gain amp.

name: TS9DX +
description:
The Turbo Tube Screamer's Plus mode: the classic circuit with more gain and more output on top.

It keeps the mid push and adds saturation the original never had.

name: Box o' Crunch
description:
The MI Audio Crunch Box: a Marshall in a small box, with more gain than the amps it imitates.

Mid-forward, aggressive and very direct. One of the better amp-in-a-box distortions.

name: OD 250 Gray
description:
The original grey DOD 250, which sounds slightly different from the reissue and costs a great deal more because of it.

Yngwie Malmsteen used one in front of a Marshall, which is most of why anybody still looks for them.

name: Horizon Precision Drive
description:
The Horizon Devices Precision Drive, designed by Misha Mansoor specifically for modern metal.

It has a noise gate built in and an attack control that sharpens the pick transient, which is the whole reason it exists — it makes fast downpicking on a downtuned guitar readable. Nothing older does that job.

name: Compulsion Distortion LP
description:
The Fulltone OCD in its low-peak setting: less gain, more headroom, and a cleaner, more open response.

The OCD's trick is MOSFET clipping, which behaves more like a valve stage than diodes do, so it stays dynamic instead of compressing flat.

name: Hoodoo Drive
description:
The Voodoo Lab Overdrive, a warm low-gain pedal in the Tube Screamer family with a flatter midrange.

Made by the company better known for power supplies.

name: Compulsion Distortion HP
description:
The OCD in high-peak mode — considerably more gain and a bigger midrange, which is the setting the pedal is famous for.

It sounds like an amp rather than a pedal, which is the whole reason it sold in the numbers it did.

name: TS9DX Hot
description:
The Turbo Tube Screamer in Hot mode, which is the most extreme of its four settings.

Considerably more gain than a TS9, with the low end opened up so it stops behaving like a boost and starts behaving like a distortion.

name: DS1 Distortion
description:
The BOSS DS-1. Orange, cheap, sold in absurd numbers, and widely dismissed by people who have never heard one set up properly.

It is brighter and harder-edged than a Tube Screamer with far more gain, and it has a midrange scoop that makes it sound thin on its own. Through a real amp with the tone rolled back it is the sound of an enormous number of records.

Kurt Cobain, Steve Vai and Joe Satriani have all used one.

name: DS1 Distortion Mod
description:
A modified DS-1, which is the second most modified pedal after the RAT.

The usual targets are the scooped midrange and the fizzy top end, and this version has more body and less of both.

name: MCMLXXXI Drive
description:
The 1981 Inventions DRV — a modern take on the RAT idea with more clarity and a more usable tone control.

It keeps the hard-clipped grind and loses most of the fizz.

name: Sonic Drive
description:
The Maxon SD-9 Sonic Distortion — a Tube Screamer relative with a much flatter midrange and a lot more gain.

Where the Screamer humps the mids, this one leaves them alone, which makes it a better standalone distortion and a worse boost.

name: Valve Screamer VS9
description:
The TS9 — the Tube Screamer that replaced the 808, with a different output section that makes it slightly brighter and more aggressive.

Which of the two is better has occupied forums for thirty years. The honest answer is that they are very close and the 9 has a touch more edge.

name: Maxoff 808
description:
The Maxon OD-808. Maxon actually built the original Tube Screamers for Ibanez, so this is the same pedal from the company whose hands it came out of.

Marginally smoother than the Ibanez-badged version, and the two are closer than the price difference suggests.

name: Klone Chiron
description:
The Klon Centaur, and the strangest story in pedals: Bill Finnegan built them by hand, charged a few hundred dollars, and the used price is now in the thousands.

What it does is add gain without changing what the guitar sounds like. The clean signal runs alongside the distorted one, so the note keeps its body and top end while the overdrive sits underneath — which is why it is called transparent and why people find it hard to describe.

As a clean boost with the gain right down it is close to perfect. That is how most people use it.

name: Esoteric Bass RCB
description:
The bass version of the RC Booster, with the low end left intact rather than filtered away.

A clean boost that does not thin out a bass guitar, which most guitar boosts do immediately.

name: BB Pre AT
description:
The Andy Timmons version of the BB Preamp: more gain, more midrange, and a smoother top end than the standard pedal.

Voiced for sustained lead playing rather than rhythm.

name: Griddle Cake
description:
The Crowther Hot Cake, made in New Zealand since the seventies and one of the first boutique overdrives anywhere.

It keeps the low end where most overdrives cut it, so it thickens rather than tightens. A very different answer from the Tube Screamer's.

name: Bosom Boost
description:
Friedman's Buxom Boost — a clean boost with a slight low-mid lift, built by an amp maker for pushing his own amps.

It adds weight rather than gain, which is the useful thing when an amp is already distorting enough.

name: OD-One Overdrive
description:
The BOSS OD-1, the first pedal BOSS ever made and the original asymmetrical overdrive.

Two knobs and almost no gain. It is a boost that adds warmth rather than a distortion, and it is the ancestor of the SD-1 and everything like it.

name: Nobelium OVD-1
description:
A low-gain overdrive with a single spectrum control in place of a conventional tone stack, which sweeps the whole voicing rather than cutting one end.

Very transparent and very flat, and much used by session players for exactly that reason.

name: Sunrise Splendor Hi-Cut
description:
The Morning Glory with its high-cut option engaged, which rounds off the top end.

For a bright amp or a bright guitar, where the standard voicing is too much.

name: Gauss Drive
description:
Mesa's Flux-Drive: an overdrive built by an amp company to sit in front of its own amps.

Tight low end and a forward midrange, made for pushing a Rectifier rather than replacing it.

name: Sunrise Splendor
description:
The JHS Morning Glory: a Bluesbreaker descendant, low gain and very open, with a bright switch for cutting through.

Designed to sit under what the amp is already doing rather than replace it.

name: Integral Pre
description:
TC Electronic's Integrated Preamp: a clean, high-headroom front end with EQ, built to sit at the start of a rack rig.

More a tone-shaping stage than a drive: headroom and EQ, with distortion left to whatever comes after it.

name: PI Fuzz - Triangle
description:
The Triangle Muff, named for the layout of its knobs and the first version Electro-Harmonix made.

The brightest and least scooped of the Muffs, with a more open low end than the ones that followed. The closest a Big Muff gets to sounding like an amp.

name: PI Fuzz - Ram's Head
basedOn: Electro-Harmonix '70s Big Muff Pi Ram's Head
description:
The Ram's Head, the second Big Muff, and the one Gilmour used.

Darker and more scooped than the Triangle, with a thick midrange dip that lets a lead sit above a mix without fighting it. The most sought-after Muff by a distance.

name: Colortone Booster
description:
The Colorsound Power Boost, which is a treble booster that kept the bass — the thing everyone wished a treble booster did.

Gilmour used one for years. It is really a preamp: it adds level and a broad, warm lift and lets the amp do the distorting.

name: Colortone OD
description:
The Colorsound Overdriver, the Power Boost's louder relative, with enough output to push almost any amp into distortion.

Rough, loud and completely unsubtle. Jeff Beck used one.

name: MOSFET Distortion
description:
The Ibanez Mostortion — MOSFET clipping and a real three-band EQ, and a quiet favourite of Nashville session players for decades.

It stays clean and natural at low gain in a way most distortion pedals cannot.

name: PI Fuzz - Russian
description:
The Russian Muff, built in Sovtek's factory when Electro-Harmonix had moved production east.

Darker, woollier and less aggressive than the American versions, with a softer top end. The sound of a lot of nineties alternative records.

name: Super Fuzz
description:
The Univox Super-Fuzz: an enormous, octave-tinged fuzz with a tone switch that scoops the midrange into oblivion.

Pete Townshend used one, and so did most of the bands who later decided guitars should be louder than everything else. It is more of an event than an effect.

name: Tube Drive 5-Knob
basedOn: Butler Tube Driver / Dean Markley Overlord
description:
The five-knob Tube Driver, with a bias control that starves the valve.

Turn it down and the pedal starts to sag, splutter and fall apart in a musically useful way — the sound of a valve being asked for more than it has.

name: 77 Custom OD
basedOn: MXR M77 Custom Badass Modified O.D.
description:
The MXR Custom Badass Modified O.D. — a Tube Screamer with the modifications already done and a bass boost switch.

More low end, more gain and more output than the pedal it is based on, for a fraction of a boutique price.

name: Angry Chuck
description:
The JHS Angry Charlie, voiced after a JCM800 with a three-band EQ to shape it.

One of the better Marshall-in-a-box pedals, and it takes a boost in front of it well.

name: Guardian Photon Speed
description:
The Greer Lightspeed: an extremely low-gain overdrive meant to be left on all the time.

It adds a little compression and a little sparkle and almost no distortion. A pedal you notice when you turn it off.

name: Paradigm Shifter
description:
Barber's Gain Changer, built around a control that alters the gain STRUCTURE rather than the amount — how hard the stages hit each other.

An unusual design, and it covers more ground than its size suggests.

name: PI Fuzz - Bass
description:
The Deluxe Bass Big Muff — the Muff circuit with the low end kept rather than filtered away, and a blend control so the clean signal stays underneath.

That blend is the whole point: fuzz on a bass without losing the note.

name: NoAmp Bass DI
description:
A direct box for bass rather than a model of a pedal: the sound of a bass going straight to the desk with no amp in the chain.

That is how an enormous number of bass parts are actually recorded, and it is a legitimate sound rather than a compromise.

name: NoAmp Bass Pre
description:
A bass preamp with EQ and no amplifier modelling behind it — shaping and level, straight to the desk.

For the very common case where the bass never goes near a speaker.

name: Royal Bass DI
description:
The Noble bass preamp and DI — a valve preamp built for recording bass straight to the desk.

Warm, expensive and used on a great many records where the bass never went near an amp.
